passages.t: Good figs: the exiles God will plant again
passages.happening:
After Nebuchadnezzar carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, with the officials of Judah and the craftsmen and metalsmiths, the LORD showed Jeremiah two baskets of figs set in front of the temple (verse 1). ‘One basket had very good figs, like those that ripen early, but the other basket contained very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten’ (verse 2). God asks what he sees, and Jeremiah answers: figs, the good very good and the bad very bad (verse 3).

God says that he regards the exiles sent to the land of the Chaldeans as good, like the good figs (verse 5). ‘I will keep My eyes on them for good and will return them to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them’ (verse 6). ‘I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the LORD’ (verse 7). They will be his people and he their God, for they will return to him with all their heart (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The vision is dated after the deportation of 597 BC. Babylon took the king, his mother, his officials, the leading men, and the craftsmen and smiths, the people who could make weapons or organize resistance. Those left behind in Jerusalem may well have thought the exiles were the ones God had judged, and themselves the ones he had spared.

Figs were a staple food, eaten fresh, dried or pressed into cakes. The first figs of the season, ripening in early summer, were a prized delicacy. Baskets set before the temple suggest offerings of firstfruits.

The promise of verse 6 uses the words of Jeremiah's call: build and plant, not tear down and uproot. Verse 7 looks ahead to the new covenant: God himself will give them a heart to know him.
passages.later: Kings records that Nebuchadnezzar took ‘all the craftsmen and metalsmiths’, leaving only the poorest of the land (2 Kings 24:14). Ezekiel, one of those exiles, received the same promise: ‘I will give them singleness of heart’ (Ezekiel 11:19).
passages.asks: Those who were taken into exile were the ones God promised to plant again. Ask whether you have read your own hardship as proof that God has rejected you. And ask what it would mean for God to give you a heart to know him.

passages.t: Bad figs: Zedekiah and those who stayed
passages.happening:
‘But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten,’ says the LORD (verse 8), so he will deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem left in the land, and those living in Egypt (verse 8).

God will make them a horror and a disgrace among all the kingdoms of the earth, a byword and a curse wherever he scatters them (verse 9). He will send sword, famine and plague against them until they are gone from the land he gave their fathers (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Zedekiah and his officials went on resisting God's word through Jeremiah, as chapters 37 and 38 tell, while the exiles were called to accept what had happened and seek God in Babylon (chapter 29). The judgment on the bad figs is a judgment on that refusal.

Those in Egypt included people who had gone there earlier, such as King Jehoahaz in 609 BC, and many more would flee there after Jerusalem fell, taking Jeremiah with them.

The vision turns the expected order upside down. The ones who seemed spared were not the ones God would build up. Circumstances were not a sign of God's favor.
passages.later: The law had warned that a disobedient people would become ‘an object of horror, scorn, and ridicule among all the nations’ (Deuteronomy 28:37). Jesus warned against reading disaster as a sign of guilt (Luke 13:4-5).
passages.hard:
Is God simply playing favorites, choosing one group and cursing another?

It can look that way, and the chapter gives no list showing that the exiles deserved better. Some readers see here pure grace: God chooses to make a new beginning with people who have already been through judgment. Others note that the bad figs are marked by their response, since Zedekiah and his officials kept resisting God's word (chapters 37 and 38), while the exiles were called to accept what had happened and seek God in Babylon (chapter 29). Both belong together. The good figs are good because God regards them so and promises to change their hearts, and the bad figs are rejected for a refusal the rest of the book records.

The chapter is also a warning against reading circumstances as proof of God's favor. Those who seemed spared were not. It concerns two groups in Judah in 597 BC, and it is no key for sorting any people today into good and bad.
passages.asks: Those who seemed safe were the ones God judged. Ask whether you have mistaken comfort for God's approval. And ask what refusal in you might be keeping you from the new heart God promises.
